Finitum Non Capax Infiniti
fee-NEE-toom nohn KAH-pahks in-FEE-nee-tee
Latin theological axiom (Christology / Reformed distinctive)
Latin finitum (the finite, that which is bounded) + non (not) + capax (capable of containing, able to hold; from capere, to take, contain, comprehend) + infiniti (of the infinite, genitive of infinitum); the principle that the finite is not capable of containing, comprehending, or circumscribing the infinite; in Reformed-Lutheran Christological debate it was the Reformed counter-axiom to the Lutheran finitum capax infiniti (the finite is capable of the infinite), which Lutherans invoked to ground the bodily presence of Christ in every celebration of the Supper

Biblical Definition

The axiom finitum non capax infiniti — the finite cannot contain the infinite — names a principle deeply rooted in Scripture's theology proper. When Solomon dedicates the temple, he asks: “Will God indeed dwell on the earth? Behold, heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain You — how much less this temple which I have built” (1 Kgs 8:27). The infinitude of God bursts every finite container: not heaven, not the highest heaven, certainly not a building. God does not dwell as creatures dwell, bounded by the dimensions of a place. Paul carries the same logic into his Areopagus address: “The God who made the world and all things in it — since He is Lord of heaven and earth — does not dwell in temples made with hands” (Acts 17:24). The finite category of “spatial containment” does not apply to the infinite God. In Christology, Colossians 2:9 affirms that “in Him dwells all the fullness of the deity bodily” — a statement the Reformed tradition reads as a miracle of the hypostatic union rather than as an abolition of the Creator-creature distinction. The finite human nature of Christ does not contain the infinite divine nature; rather, the divine Person assumes the human nature without the infinite being absorbed into or contained by the finite. The extra Calvinisticum teaches that the divine Son continued to govern creation even while incarnate — the infinite was not compressed into the finite but condescended into it while remaining unbounded.

Webster 1828 Definition

FINITUM NON CAPAX INFINITI: Latin axiom, “the finite cannot contain the infinite”; the Reformed counter-principle to the Lutheran finitum capax infiniti; grounds the Creator-creature distinction in theology proper, the extra Calvinisticum in Christology, and the Reformed doctrine of Christ's spiritual (not bodily) presence in the Lord's Supper, in contrast to Lutheran ubiquity and Catholic transubstantiation.

expand to see more

FINITUM NON CAPAX INFINITI. Latin. The finite is not capable of containing the infinite. The governing axiom of Reformed theology proper and Christology: God's infinitude cannot be circumscribed by any finite thing; the finite human nature of Christ does not “contain” the infinite divine nature in the sense of becoming the vessel that defines or limits it.

The Lutheran axiom finitum capax infiniti (“the finite is capable of the infinite”) was invoked to ground the doctrine of ubiquity (the body of Christ present everywhere by virtue of the communicatio idiomatum) and therefore the bodily presence of Christ in every Supper celebration worldwide simultaneously. The Reformed disputed this: the doctrine of ubiquity for the human nature contradicts the real humanity Christ took, which is a locatable, glorified body ascended and sessioned at the Father's right hand (Heb 9:24; Acts 3:21).

The extra Calvinisticum (the “beyond” of Calvin) is the positive doctrinal correlate: the divine Son, even while incarnate, continued to sustain creation, govern providence, and exist beyond the limits of the assumed human nature. The infinite was not compressed into the finite; it condescended into genuine embodied human life while remaining, as to the divine nature, illimitable.

Practically: in the Lord's Supper, the Reformed hold that Christ's glorified body is in heaven at the right hand of the Father (Acts 3:21; Heb 8:1), not physically present in or under the bread and wine. The Supper is no less a real communion with Christ for this: the Spirit lifts the believing soul to the ascended Christ in a spiritual feeding that is truly Christ Himself, not merely a memorial idea.

Key Scripture

1 Kgs 8:27 — "But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?"

Acts 17:24 — "God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands;"

Col 2:9 — "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily."

Isa 40:12 — "Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and meted out heaven with the span, and comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales, and the hills in a balance?"

Modern Corruption

Lutheran ubiquity doctrine inverts the axiom with finitum capax infiniti, teaching that Christ's glorified body can be present everywhere the Supper is celebrated simultaneously; Catholic transubstantiation likewise localizes the infinite in the finite elements of bread and wine through the theory of substance change.

expand to see more

The Lutheran doctrine of ubiquity was developed to ground the real bodily presence of Christ in the bread and wine of every Lord's Supper celebrated simultaneously around the world. The argument required that Christ's human nature, glorified and exalted, received the divine attribute of omnipresence through the communicatio idiomatum — the communication of attributes between the divine and human natures of Christ. This inverts the Reformed axiom: the finite human nature is made capable of containing the infinite attribute of omnipresence. The Reformed response is that the communicatio idiomatum does not transfer divine attributes to the human nature (which would destroy the real, finite, glorified humanity of Christ) but names the personal actions of the one Christ who acts according to His divine and human natures. A human nature that is omnipresent is not a human nature; ubiquity requires a docetic Christology that effectively abolishes the genuinely finite human nature Christ retains in His glorification.

Catholic transubstantiation localizes Christ differently: through the words of consecration the substance of bread and wine is changed into the substance of Christ's body and blood, while the accidents (appearance, taste, texture) remain. The finite elements become the infinite Christ. The Reformed objection applies here also: the theory requires that a finite material substance can contain or become the infinite Person of Christ, which contradicts both the Creator-creature distinction and the doctrine of Christ's glorified body ascended to heaven. Hebrews 9:24 places Christ in heaven itself, not in earthly tabernacles; Acts 3:21 speaks of heaven retaining Him until the restoration of all things. The Supper's real spiritual communion with the exalted Christ (affirmed) does not require the finite bread to contain the infinite Lord (denied).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin finitum (the finite, bounded) + non capax (not capable of containing) + infiniti (of the infinite); the axiom arose explicitly in the Marburg Colloquy (1529) between Luther and Zwingli/Oecolampadius and was refined in the subsequent Reformed-Lutheran controversy over the Lord's Supper through the 16th and 17th centuries.

expand to see more

Latin capax — capable of containing, holding, or comprehending; from capere (to take, seize, contain); the image is physical: a vessel has a capacitas (capacity) for what it holds; the axiom denies that finite creaturely vessels — whether temples, bodies, or bread — have the capacitas to contain God's infinitude

Marburg Colloquy (1529) — the failed meeting between Luther and Zwingli/Oecolampadius over the Lord's Supper; they agreed on 14 of 15 articles but parted over the presence of Christ's body in the Supper; the Reformed finitum non capax infiniti and the Lutheran finitum capax infiniti crystallized as the formal dividing statement

John Calvin (1509–1564) — Institutes IV.17 and his debates with Westphal and Heshusius; Calvin's most sustained development of the axiom in Christological and sacramental application; the extra Calvinisticum (the divine Son beyond the flesh even while incarnate) is the positive counterpart to the negative axiom

Heinrich Bullinger (1504–1575) and the Second Helvetic Confession (1566) — the Reformed consensus document that refined the position: Christ's body is in heaven; He is truly present in the Supper spiritually by the Spirit; the finite bread does not contain the infinite Christ

Herman Bavinck (1854–1921), Reformed Dogmatics II — the 20th-century systematic treatment; Bavinck extends the axiom to all of theology proper: every divine attribute (omnipotence, omniscience, omnipresence, eternity) names an infinite perfection no finite creature can contain or comprehend, which is why all creaturely knowledge of God is accommodated, revelatory knowledge given from above, not metaphysical ascent from below

Usage

"The axiom has its most immediate preaching application in worship: the living God whom we approach in prayer and praise is not contained within our liturgical forms, our buildings, our denominational tradition, or our imaginative conceptions of Him. Solomon's prayer at the temple's dedication models the right posture: the temple is the LORD's dwelling place by His own gracious choice, yet it cannot contain Him. Worship approaches the infinite God through His own appointed means, but without the idolatrous assumption that the means contain Him."

"In Christology, the axiom guards the real humanity of Christ: if the finite human nature were made to hold the infinite divine nature without remainder, the human nature ceases to be genuinely finite and therefore genuinely human. Christ's ascended body is a real glorified human body in a real location — the right hand of the Father. His divine nature is everywhere; His human nature is in the place of honor. The two natures are united in one Person without confusion or change (Chalcedon), but the finite human nature does not become infinite by the union."

"In the Lord's Supper, the axiom redirects the believer's eyes upward: the bread and cup are signs, ordained by Christ, through which the Spirit lifts the believer's soul to commune with the ascended Christ Himself in heaven. The Supper is not a calling down of Christ from heaven into earthly elements but a Spirit-granted ascent to the Christ who is in heaven. This is why the Reformed Supper is no less a real feeding — it is real communion with the real Christ, received not through physical presence in bread but through Spirit-given faith in the one who sits at the Father's right hand."
